segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, my brothers and sisters, beloved and longed for, my joy and crown, stand firm in the Lord in this way, beloved.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I urge Euodia and I urge Syntyche to be of one mind in the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Yes, and I ask you also, true partner, to help these women, who contended at my side in the good news, along with Clement and the rest of my co-workers, whose names are in the book of life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: rejoice!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let your forbearance be known to all people. The Lord is near.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will stand guard over your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Finally, brothers and sisters, whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, whatever is pure, whatever is lovable, whatever is well spoken of, if there is any excellence and if there is anything worthy of praise, dwell on these things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What you learned and received and heard and saw in me, put these things into practice, and the God of peace will be with you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I rejoiced greatly in the Lord that now at last your concern for me has blossomed again; you were indeed concerned, but you had no opportunity.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not that I say this out of want, for I have learned to be self-sufficient in whatever circumstances I am in.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I know how to be brought low, and I know how to have more than enough. In each and every circumstance I have been initiated into being well fed and going hungry, into having more than enough and being in want.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I have strength for all things in the one who empowers me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Even so, you did well to share in my affliction.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And you Philippians yourselves know that in the early days of the good news, when I left Macedonia, no assembly shared with me in an account of giving and receiving except you alone;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for even in Thessalonica you sent something for my need, once and then again.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not that I seek the gift; rather, I seek the fruit that accrues to your account.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I have received everything in full and have more than enough. I am filled, now that I have received from Epaphroditus what came from you, a fragrant aroma, an acceptable sacrifice, pleasing to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And my God will fill your every need according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To our God and Father be the glory to the ages of the ages. Amen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Greet every holy one in Christ Jesus. The brothers and sisters who are with me greet you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: All the holy ones greet you, especially those of Caesar's household.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.

notes.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of siblings or fellow members. Paul goes on at once to name two women of the community, so 'brothers' alone would now suggest a narrower audience than his readers understood. Many recent translations make the same choice; others keep 'brothers' with a footnote.

The word means someone yoked together with another, a close partner in work. Paul does not name the person, and the Philippians evidently knew who was meant. Some scholars take the word as a proper name, Syzygus, with a play on its meaning ('you who are a partner in fact as in name'), but the name is not attested elsewhere.

The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' has since become a purely religious term and a book title. Many modern translations already alternate between the two renderings.

The Greek can mean near in time (the Lord's coming is soon, as in 3:20) or near in presence (the Lord is close to those who call on him, as in Psalm 145:18). The sentence may be read with what precedes or what follows, and Paul may intend both senses. The rendering leaves the question open as the Greek does.

Several terms in this list, and this one above all, belong to the common vocabulary of Greek moral teaching, not to the special vocabulary of the Septuagint. This is the only place Paul uses the word, the standard Greek term for moral excellence. He appears to be telling the Philippians to take account of whatever their wider culture rightly recognizes as good.

The word was the standard term, prized especially by Stoic and Cynic teachers, for a person who is independent of circumstances and needs nothing from outside. Most translations use 'content', which is a recognized sense, but it loses the echo a first-century reader would have heard. Verse 13 then gives the twist: Paul's sufficiency comes not from himself but from the one who empowers him.

notes.traditional: I have learned the secret / I am instructed
notes.note: The verb is the technical term for initiation into a mystery cult, used only here in the New Testament. Paul uses it figuratively: plenty and want alike are rites he has been through. Most translations paraphrase as 'learned the secret', which conveys the sense but hides the image.

notes.phrase: I have strength for all things
notes.note: The verb means to be strong or to have power for something. 'All things' looks back to the circumstances just listed, hunger and plenty, want and abundance; the sentence is about enduring any situation, not accomplishing any goal. 'I can do all things' is a fair rendering and is the mainstream one, though it is often read out of context. Later manuscripts add 'Christ' after 'the one who empowers me', whence the familiar 'through Christ'; the earliest text leaves him unnamed.

A first-century hearer knew this word as a civic gathering of citizens and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is near-universal in English and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' wherever the word occurs.

notes.phrase: an account of giving and receiving
notes.traditional: in the matter of giving and receiving
notes.note: Paul uses the language of business throughout this passage. 'Account of giving and receiving' was a bookkeeping expression for credits and debits; 'fruit that accrues to your account' in verse 17 is the language of profit or interest; and 'I have received in full' in verse 18 is the formula written on receipts. He describes the Philippians' gift as a partnership, with the return credited to them by God.

notes.traditional: an odour of a sweet smell / a fragrant offering
notes.note: This is the Septuagint's stock phrase for the smoke of a sacrifice rising pleasingly to God (for example Genesis 8:21 and often in Leviticus). Paul turns from commercial to temple language: the money sent to him is in truth an offering made to God.

notes.phrase: to the ages of the ages
notes.note: The Greek is a Semitic-style superlative, literally 'into the ages of the ages', meaning through all ages without end. 'For ever and ever' gives the sense and is the usual rendering. The literal form is kept here because this translation preserves such turns of phrase where the Greek has them.

Paul uses this word for every member of the community, as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. 'Saint' now suggests a canonized individual or a person of exceptional virtue. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

This was the usual term for the emperor's large staff of slaves and freed slaves who ran the imperial administration, in Rome and in the provinces. It does not mean members of the emperor's family. Philippi was a Roman colony, and a greeting from believers in imperial service would have carried particular weight there.

candidates.reason: The plural addressed to mixed communities occurs throughout the letters and Acts, and translators divide between 'brothers', 'brothers and sisters' and 'friends'; it needs one policy.
A thematic word in Philippians and Romans (mindset, attitude, concern) that translations render very variously, which obscures Paul's deliberate repetition.
The doxology formula and related phrases ('this age', 'forever') recur across the New Testament, and a decision is needed on literal 'ages' versus 'forever'.
It is frequent across books and is rendered variously as tribulation, affliction, trouble, distress or suffering, with 'tribulation' carrying heavy later theological baggage.
It denotes a victor's or festal wreath, not a royal diadem; 'crown' recurs in Paul, James, 1 Peter and Revelation and can mislead about the image.
